newsitem.title: UK: Sinn Fein say Loyalists behind death threats.
newsitem.headline: Sinn Fein say Loyalists behind death threats.

text.p: A key figure in the IRA's Sinn Fein political wing, Alex Maskey, said on Sunday that police had warned him of a death threat by suspected pro-British Loyalists in a fresh spate of violence in British Northern Ireland.

Sinn Fein said similar warnings were given by police to its president Gerry Adams and its chief negotiator Martin McGuinness some three weeks ago, and the party was taking them seriously in light of two recent attacks on other leading republicans.
The outlawed Ulster Freedom Fighters guerrilla group was blamed in media reports for a failed bomb attack on a senior Sinn Fein member in Londonderry city on Saturday.
The same Loyalist group, so-called because it is "loyal" to British rule, is also suspected of planting a booby-trap bomb that wounded a leading Irish republican in Belfast last week.
Commanders of Loyalist milita have refused to state whether their two-year-truce has ended.

But the resurgence of suspected Protestant guerrilla violence is being seen as a further blow to a peace process severely damaged last February by the Irish Republican Army's decision to end its 17-month ceasefire.
Sinn Fein spokesmen said that police did not give any information about the origin of the threats to their leaders but the party was convinced they came from Loyalist militants.
The Royal Ulster Constabulary, which does not normally comment on security for individuals, declined to comment.

Blaming "loyalist paramilitaries", Sinn Fein executive member Maskey said he was told of the death threat by police on Saturday. He said they told him "there is an imminent threat to your life...You know the routine, increase your security."
Sinn Fein chairman Gerry O'Hara said that some three weeks ago police had relayed a warning through a third party to McGuinness about imminent threat to him and Adams.
But Sinn Fein denied a British newspaper report that Adams and McGuinness were recently appointed to the Irish Republican Army's seven-person "army council" leadership.
A spokesman said: "There is no basis for it whatsoever."

The Sunday Times report, which quoted unnamed British security and intelligence sources, said the IRA leadership would call an open-ended tactical ceasefire in February but would give the go-ahead for more anti-British violence in the meantime.

Suspected Loyalist violence, seen as revenge attacks for recent IRA hositilities, has fuelled speculation that "mainstream" Protestant parties may seek to have Loyalist politicians expelled from current multi-party peace talks.
The political wings of the Protestant guerrillas have seats in peace talks chaired by former U.S.senator George Mitchell on condition that their military allies maintain a ceasefire.
Sinn Fein is barred from the talks because the IRA, which is fighting against British rule, refuses to call a new ceasefire.
